Chapter 7: The Myth of the Gifted Child
Picture this. You’re sitting in a packed auditorium, surrounded by proud parents and excited kids, all waiting for the big “gifted and talented” awards. The spotlight lands on a handful of children—those with sky-high test scores and minds that seem to work at lightning speed. The message? Some kids are just born exceptional. And everyone else, well, they have to work that much harder to keep up.
But underneath all the applause and certificates, there’s a quieter story—a truth that’s easy to miss. Intelligence isn’t just a number, or a label handed out in elementary school. It’s way more complicated than that.
For years, schools have leaned on tests to decide who’s “gifted,” believing that early achievement somehow predicts success for life. But here’s something researchers discovered after following those same kids as they grew up: the early superstars didn’t always stay ahead. In fact, plenty of five- and six-year-olds who seemed destined for greatness just kind of blended in later on. And those who were overlooked? Many of them found their stride and started to shine much later.
Let me share a real-life example. In one classroom, there was a quiet girl who struggled to read while her classmates zipped through chapter books. Each mistake chipped away at her confidence, and teachers worried she’d always be behind. But with a little patience, encouragement, and the right kind of support, she slowly caught up. By the time she reached middle school, she loved reading—and her curiosity and determination lit up every room.
Stories like these show that intelligence isn’t something you’re simply born with, or something you can measure in a single moment. Kids grow, change, and develop at their own pace. Early tests often miss hidden strengths and talents just waiting to emerge. And when we label and sort children too soon, we can actually make them feel anxious or discouraged—like they’re stuck in a box.
In another family, a boy who wasn’t picked for the gifted program felt left out. He started to believe he just wasn’t “smart enough.” His parents tried to reassure him, but what really made a difference was helping him find actual joy in learning. They let him explore topics that excited him, ask questions, and celebrate his progress—not just the end result.
Most of us don’t realize just how much potential is shaped by encouragement, opportunity, and the environment around us. The whole idea of the “gifted child” overlooks the incredible power of growth, effort, and resilience.
So, what’s the real takeaway here? Every child has unique strengths, and you just can’t capture their potential with a single test or label. When we nurture curiosity and perseverance, we give every child a real chance to thrive—no matter when or how their talents start to shine.
